title: Polesia
summary: Polesia, also known as Palessie, Polissia, or Polesie, is a significant natural and historical region in [[eastern-europe|Eastern Europe]], prominently featuring the Belarus–Ukraine border and parts of eastern Poland. It is recognized for its extensive forested areas and marshlands, particularly relevant to Ukraine's geography and history.

sections.heading: Geographical Extent
paragraphs: Polesia is one of the largest forested regions in Europe, situated in the southwestern part of the Eastern-European Lowland, specifically the Polesian Lowland. It encompasses the Bug River valley in Poland and the [[pripyat-river|Pripyat River]] valley in [[western-ukraine|Western Ukraine]]. Historically, the westernmost area of Polesia, near Brest, Belarus, was part of the Podlachia region. According to the late 19th-century Geographical Dictionary of the Kingdom of Poland, Polesia is defined as a triangle formed by the cities of Brest, Mogilev, and [[kyiv|Kyiv]].

The central swampy areas of Polesia are referred to as the Pinsk Marshes. Following the [[chernobyl-disaster|Chernobyl disaster]], significant portions of this region were contaminated, leading to the establishment of the [[chernobyl-exclusion-zone|Chernobyl Exclusion Zone]] and the [[rivne-oblast|Polesie]] State Radioecological Reserve, which includes [[administrative-territorial-entity-of-ukraine|areas in Ukraine]] north-northwest of Kyiv.

sections.heading: Cultural and Historical Significance
paragraphs: The name Polesia derives from the East Slavic root les, meaning 'forest', combined with the prefix po-, which denotes location. The inhabitants of Polesia are known as Paleshuks.

Historically, the region was inhabited by the Milograd culture and the Neuri in ancient times. In the late Middle Ages, Polesia became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569. It transitioned to Russian control during the late 18th-century Partitions of Poland. From 1921 to 1939, Polesia was largely under Polish governance, with the eastern portion becoming part of the Byelorussian SSR, which established the Polesia Region in 1938.

sections.heading: Geographical Features
paragraphs: Polesia is characterized by its marshy landscape along the Pripyat River, spanning Southern Belarus, Northern [[ukraine|Ukraine]] (including the Volyn, [[rivne|Rivne]], [[zhytomyr|Zhytomyr]], Kyiv, and [[chernihiv|Chernihiv]] Oblasts), and parts of Poland. The region is a flatland within the drainage basins of the Western Bug and [[pripyat|Pripyat]] rivers, which are connected by the [[dnieper|Dnieper]]-Bug Canal, constructed during the reign of Stanislaus II of Poland.

Key tributaries of the Pripyat River include the Horyn, Stokhid, Styr, Ptsich, and Yaselda rivers. Major towns in the Pripyat basin consist of Pinsk, Stolin, and Davyd-Haradok. From the 1960s to the 1980s, extensive marshlands were drained for agricultural purposes.

sections.heading: Impact of the Chernobyl Disaster
paragraphs: The Chernobyl disaster had a profound impact on Polesia, resulting in widespread radioactive contamination. The most severely affected areas include the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone and the adjacent Polesie State Radioecological Reserve, with some regions deemed unsuitable for habitation.

sections.heading: Tourism and Conservation
paragraphs: The Polish segment of Polesia features the Polesie National Park, established in 1990, which spans 97.6 square kilometers. This park, along with adjacent areas, forms part of the UNESCO-designated West Polesie Biosphere Reserve, which borders the Shatsk Biosphere Reserve in Ukraine. Additionally, the region's wooden architectural structures were added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on January 30, 2004.
